messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur Vance was seventy-three when he finally sat across from a therapist, but the story of his distress began decades earlier in the press gallery of the Metropolitan Convention Center. He had been arranging his notes for the afternoon briefing when the steel truss above the north section groaned and gave way. The collapse was sudden, leaving a cloud of plaster and splintered timber in its wake. Arthur remembered the sharp, metallic tang of dust settling on his tongue, the colorless glass shards skittering across the floor like shrapnel, and the way the unpredictability of the failure caught him off guard. He had come to believe that the gallery’s architecture was holding its breath, waiting to fail again. His checklist scores settled in the seventy-four range, mirroring the quiet intensity of his daily experience. In the weeks that followed, Arthur noticed that certain photographs from that day pulled him back into the scene. When he viewed the press images showing the twisted railings and the fallen ceiling, his chest tightened as if the plaster were still falling. He began to sit with his back pressed firmly against the wall, a habit that grew into a necessity. He was certain that if he faced the room, he would miss the next warning sign. Even in his familiar house, he could not relax. His attention drifted to the sounds of the hallway, the settle of the floorboards, the creak of the stairwell, each one prompting him to wonder if someone was entering. He found himself scanning his environment for potential weapons, noting the heavy brass lamp by his desk, the letter opener on his writing table, the sharp edge of his shears, as though any of them might become dangerous if the world turned hostile. The taste that first morning stayed with him. It was the bitter, dusty flavor of emergency rations and pulverized drywall, and now, whenever he drank a specific brand of chicory coffee or ate a particularly dry rusk, the sensation would catch him in the throat. Unpredictable situations sharpened his awareness. A chair scraping too loudly across a floor, a sudden gust of wind against a window, a colleague shifting position without warning—all of them met his attention with quiet alarm. When the alarm rose too high, Arthur would freeze completely, his body still, his mind waiting for the tension to resolve. He had tried to work through it, but the work of a journalist demanded he think, and he had come to believe that if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it. So he kept his thoughts at bay, turning instead to the quiet rhythm of the register. He found himself spending money impulsively, purchasing archival papers, extra volumes of photographs, and long-term subscriptions to news feeds, the transactions offering a steady, predictable anchor alongside the past. His memories did not fade into neat summaries. They replayed like a film, the sequence of the collapse looping in his mind, sometimes so vivid that Arthur felt the weight of the debris on his shoulders as if it were happening right now. Yet, when he tried to explain it to others, he would pause, wondering if his experience was too extreme to be real. The story felt unreal, as though it had befallen a man who looked very much like him but lived in a different decade. Over time, his emotional range narrowed. He was certain he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, his joy and sorrow dulled by the constant hum of vigilance. Even his professional life shifted. He stopped attending the monthly writers’ luncheon at the downtown hotel, not because he disliked the company, but because the unpredictable clatter of silverware and the sudden announcements in the hall made it difficult to stay grounded. His work continued, but it felt distant, as though nothing in his life held the same meaning it once did. What finally brought Arthur to seek help was a morning when he stood in his kitchen, a cup of bitter coffee in his hand, listening to the quiet house and realizing that the vigilance had become his daily rhythm. He did not want to lose the clarity his work had given him, but he wanted to stop carrying the weight of the gallery with him into every room. He hoped, perhaps for the first time, that he might be able to let the film stop playing without feeling as though the ceiling would fall again.
